Various strategies for lignin valorization. 19 M. Zhou et al. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 156 (2022) 111986 Fig. 8). 6.2.1. Biological route In nature, lignin can be degraded by many ligninolytic microorganisms. Many fungi (e.g., white rot fungi) [39] and bacteria (e.g., Rhodococcus opacus) [131] are able to efficiently delignify lignocellulosic biomass. Lignin can be in vivo depolymerized by a broad enzymatic machine into aromatic compounds. The enzymatic arsenal includes laccase, manganese peroxidase (MnP), versatile peroxidase (VP), heme-dependent lignin peroxidase (LigP), dye-decolorizing peroxidase (DyP), β-etherase, aryl alcohol oxidase, and glyoxal oxidase. Subsequently, these compounds are metabolized via the β-ketoadipate, phenylacetic acid, and homogentisate pathways, and finally enter into the TCA or another cycle to biosynthesize various valuable products [131]. It has been reported that *Pandoraea* sp. B-6 can assist in the further depolymerization of lignin remaining in the solid residues from ChCl: LA-pretreated rice straw [132]. FTIR and HSQC NMR results revealed that *Pandoraea* sp. B-6 further promoted the fragmentation of the G units in lignin after DES pretreatment. A more recent study demonstrated that the DES waste extraction liquor from lignin could be converted into microbial lipid by *Rhodotorula glutinis* fermentation [46]. Additionally, metabolic engineering and synthetic biology are usually used to tailor and improve the ligninolytic microbe's ability to degrade and metabo- lize lignin [131]. Despite noteworthy development, the biological upgrading of lignin is still challenging because the overall efficiency is relatively low. The biological conversion of lignin normally is very time-consuming (a few days or weeks) and inefficient as compared to other depolymerization routes. Apart from the microbial depolymerization, enzymatic depolymerization of lignin is a promising alternative strategy. Strikingly, some laccases exhibit satisfactory biocompatibility with many DESs. The activity of Trametes versicolor laccase was preserved, and particularly enhanced up to 200% in certain DESs [133]. Although the activity and stability of some laccases were decreased in some DESs [134], their biocompatibility with DESs could be improved by protein engineering strategies, such as direct evolution. It is a rational speculation given that the laccase activity in ionic liquids can be improved by direct evolution [135] and that DESs resemble ionic liquids. Further protein engineering studies should be conducted to verify this speculation. Laccase can also degrade lignin into aromatic chemicals in aqueous ionic liquids [136]. Thus, it is reasonable to speculate that laccase can oxidatively degrade lignin into value-added compounds when using DESs as the reaction medium. Additionally, considering that DESs show excellent capacity for lignin fractionation from biomass, a consolidated process can be envisioned by conducting lignin fractionation and further conversion in the same DES by laccase oxidation. Similarly, the biocompatibility of other lignin-degrading enzymes (such as laccase, MnP, VP, and LigP) with DESs should be investigated to explore more biological routes for lignin depolymerization. In the future, substantial efforts should be made to promote the biological conversion of lignin as being time-saving and efficient. 6.2.2. *Thermochemical route* Because of the aromatic structure of lignin, it is a potential precursor for the preparation of high value-added materials or chemicals via thermochemical conversion. Based on whether the catalyst is used or not, the thermochemical conversion of lignin can be classified as a non-catalytic or catalytic thermochemical transformation [100]. Non-catalytic thermochemical transformations. Pyrolysis and gasifica- tion are two main thermochemical transformation processes for lignin valorization. The pyrolysis process consists of heating lignin under an inert atmosphere at elevated temperatures (ranging from 150 to 700 °C). Lignin is later condensed into bio-oil and biochar as the major products [137]. The bio-oil is mainly composed of phenols, ketones, aldehydes, ethers, alcohols, and carboxylic acids, and can be further upgraded into other value-added chemicals. The biochar has many practical applications and is considered as a solid fuel source [138]. DES lignin has also shown impressive performance in lignin pyrol- ysis. For example, the DES lignin extracted by acidified ChCl:EG pro- duced considerable amounts of phenolic monomers after pyrolysis [25, 27]. Based on the pyrolysis performance, suitable downstream appli- cations were proposed for the varying DES lignin obtained by pyrolysis using different DESs. Lignin fractionated by ChCl:FA was recommended for use as a carbon source (e.g., biochar) due to the high percentage of pyrolysis char residue, while lignin extracted by ChCl:LA was suitable for smaller-scale chemical production because its main pyrolysis prod- ucts were volatile aromatic chemicals [86]. Compared with pyrolysis, gasification is normally conducted at even higher temperatures (>800 °C) under a reactive atmosphere (air, oxygen, or steam) to yield synthetic gas (such as CO, H2, and CH4) as the major product. These synthetic gases can further be converted into fuels or chemical products [137]. The TG-FTIR analysis showed that DES lignin (especially for ChCl:LA-fractionated) released high concentrations of gaseous products. This finding indicates its potential to serve as feedstock in gasification to produce syngas [86]. Catalytic thermochemical transformations. Catalytic thermochemical transformations mainly involve three pathways: (1) catalytic cracking/ hydrolysis (into bio-oil or biochar), (2) catalytic reduction (into phenol or benzene, toluene and xylene, or BTX) via hydrogenolysis, hydrogenation, or hydrodeoxygenation, and (3) catalytic oxidation (into vanillin, acetovanillone, or acids) [137]. Lignin bio-oil is not suitable for direct use due to its high instability, corrosive nature, low heating value, and low incompatibility with pe- troleum fuels. Therefore, the stabilization and upgrading of lignin bio- oil are necessary to optimize its energy density and molecular weight, as well as to reduce the oxygen content [45]. The removal of oxygen atoms in lignin bio-oils (by removal of the methoxy and hydroxyl group, for example) can be triggered through direct C-O hydrogenolysis, C=C hydrogenation, and hydrodeoxygenation [139]. A possible valorization pathway of DES lignin toward value-added low-molecular weight phenolic compounds has been demonstrated [93]. More recently, a one-pot procedure consisting of extraction and depolymerization of lignin by DES has been developed [140]. This strategy offers a step-efficient protocol for producing a single and valuable catechol compound from lignocellulosic biomass. The catalytic oxidation of lignin mainly produces more complex and valuable aromatic compounds with active functional groups. These functional groups include but are not limited to alcohol groups, aldehyde groups or carboxylic acid moieties. They offer many functionalization possibilities [141]. The resulted products normally are methoxy-phenolic aldehydes (vanillin, syringaldehyde, and p-hydroxy-benzaldehyde), carboxylic acids (vanillic acid and syringic acid), and ketones (acetovanillone and acetosyringone). A recent work reported an effective strategy for the catalytic conversion of lignin into versatile aromatic compounds. The H units of lignin were selectively catalyzed into methyl p-hydroxycinnamate as the sole product, with high yield and selectivity [142]. Two recent studies showed that lignin depolymerization could be accomplished through the solvolytic action of DESs (ChCl: LA or ChCl:OA) under relatively mild temperatures (80–140 °C). This depolymerization directly led to depolymerized lignin oil rich in value-added phenolic diketones [30,98]. Although no exogenous catalyst was added, the acidic environment of a DES might trigger the acid-catalyzed depolymerization of lignin. Significantly, depolymerized lignin products in DES systems contain unique diketone compounds that have not been observed after other types of acid pretreatment until now. 6.2.3. *Electrochemical route* Lignin can be selectively electrochemically depolymerized into ver- satile aromatic compounds, such as vanillin [44] and acetovanillone [11]. Electrochemical depolymerization uses renewable electricity sources and is free from toxic and/or expensive oxidizers. This depoly- merization route is green, inexpensive, and highly sustainable. 20 M. Zhou et al. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 156 (2022) 111986 Currently, a feasible electrochemical strategy for lignin depolymerization includes reductive pathways and oxidative pathways [45]. In the reductive pathway, H2 is normally used as the reductive agent for selective hydrogenolysis of lignin into phenols, while in the oxidative pathway, H2O2, O2 and their resulting reactive oxygen species (HO•, O2•−, or HOO•) play pivotal roles in the electrochemical depolymerization of lignin. Generally, three operation modes of an electrode can be considered in most electrochemical depolymerization procedures for lignin (illustrated in Fig. 8) [143]. A crucial point is a working electrolyte/reaction medium that sufficiently dissolves lignin while ensuring satisfactory conductivity for electrochemical reaction. DESs are suitable candidates due to their satisfactory lignin solubility and electric conductivity. Di Marino et al. carried out pioneering work demonstrating that ChCl:EG dissolved lignin and served as an excellent medium for further electrochemical oxidative depolymerization of lignin into low-molecular-weight aromatic compounds [44,144]. The authors achieved efficient depolymerization of lignin through simultaneous fractionation of degraded products by in situ extraction, which prevented their over-oxidation [144]. Recently, a novel catalytic oxidation system was established that consisted of a copper catalyst in oxygenated ChCl:methanol that converted lignin into acetovanillone and acetic acid with high yield and selectivity [11]. Given the ability of DESs to efficiently fractionate lignin from biomass, it is highly conceivable to develop a consolidated strategy conducting lignin fractionation and further conversion in the same DESs by electrochemical oxidation. This consolidated process will eliminate steps in lignin recovery and reduce waste generation, which thus results in greater economic feasibility for lignin valorization [145]. Despite of all these advantages, some challenges still exist in such a strategy at present: (1) the lack of understanding regarding the structure-processing relationship for DESs-based electrochemical depolymerization; (2) the underdevelopment of catalysts/electrodes that are compatible and active in DES systems; and (3) the unoptimized reaction conditions (e.g., oxidation potential) which result in products with low yield and selectivity. More efforts are required to advance the electrochemical depolymerization of lignin in DES systems. 7. Future perspectives DESs are an emerging class of green solvents that hold great promise for lignin fractionation and valorization. Although significant progress has been made in the past few years, several issues with respect to the fundamental mechanisms and technical challenges require rigorous investigations for future works. Fundamental knowledge on how DES interacts with lignin during fractionation, dissolution, and valorization should be established. An in-depth investigation is needed on the structure-function relationship of DESs during fractionation to increase efficiency is needed. The underlying mechanisms of lignin dissolution and fractionation should be elucidated at a molecular level. More comprehensive research is required to understand the intrinsic mechanism and structural transformation changes of lignin during valorization. It is well-known that the addition of the correct amount of water will reduce the viscosity of DESs and contribute to applications. However, how much water can be added to DES without disrupting the solvent's intermolecular bonding structure is non-conclusive. Data collection on how water addition affects the DES molecular framework and its interaction with lignin would provide insightful information to facilitate the application of aqueous DESs. These insights will lay a foundation for the design, selection, and application of DESs. In view of the tremendous amount of DES varieties, time- and resource-efficient screening approaches are required. At present, a vast majority of the studies involve the use of acidic DES. Other type of DESs, such as type V DESs, also show great potential in lignin fractionation and valorization. It is recommended to diversify the types of DESs adopted in lignin fractionation and valorization to fully explore the potential of DESs. Despite the direct design of DESs according to their intended purpose, which is promising, this strategy should be based on sound knowledge regrading the structure-function relationships common to DESs. Along with constantly increasing studies on DESs and applica- tions, the available data on DESs will exponentially grow. Computa- tional approaches such as machine learning, in which massive data sets are manipulated, are potent strategies to guide the selection of DESs. More efforts are required to develop effective DESs recycling tech-nologies. Changes in DES constituents, DES degradation, unexpected interactions with biomass-derived impurities that influence DES prop-erties, and slightly unstable lignin structures and properties are found during the recyclable usage of DESs. The chemical structures and fundamental properties of DESs, the elimination of unexpected in-teractions, as well as the exploration of innovative technologies to remove impurities should be further investigated to increase the overall economic efficiency of the DESs-based biorefinery. Detailed studies on the structures and properties of DESs-extracted lignin and comparison with other technical lignin are necessary. The possibility of applying DES lignin to existing lignin upgrading schemes needs to be evaluated, and the possible applications that have yet to be accomplished with the existing technical lignin should be explored. Additionally, DES lignin with tailored structures and properties can be achieved by adjusting DESs and process conditions. Currently, multiple types of upgraded lignin products such as aromatic compounds, bio-oil, biochar, nanoparticles, and smart materials have been successfully produced from the DESs-fractionated lignin in several works. However, the selectivity and yield of these upgrading routes greatly varied. Strategies to increase the usage of intended products will also be a great research direction in future works. Besides, it will also be worthwhile to explore more varieties of higher value lignin-derived commodity chemicals or materials to be converted from DESs-fractionated lignin to increase the process revenue. A consolidated strategy can be envisioned by integrating lignin fractionation and further upgrading by the use of renewable DESs into a one-pot process. This strategy maximizes the utilization of biomass and minimizes the waste and use of chemicals and catalysts, and also creates opportunities toward a sustainable and circular bio-economy. Nevertheless, some technical challenges should be overcome. Many factors must be taken into consideration, including the type of biomass and its properties, reactor types, batch or continuous operations, recycling strategies, recovery and purification of product, and elimination of side-effects, as well as the development of DES-compatible catalysts. Presently, catalysts, enzymes, or electrodes that are compatible and active in DES environments remain under-exploited. In the future work, the development of DES-compatible catalysts to fractionate and valorize lignin with high selectivity and yield should be carried out. Exploration of new enzymes or modification of existing enzymes that are compatible with DESs through protein engineering is also highly encouraged. Furthermore, extensive life-cycle assessment and techno-economic analysis of consolidated strategies are also pressing research topics to further evaluate the feasibilities of lignin fractionation and valorization. ## 8. Conclusions This review summarized the recent advances in lignin fractionation and valorization using DESs in view of newly emerging type V DESs, the underlying mechanisms to intensify strategies with DES treatment, the structure and properties of DES lignin, the mechanism of lignin dissolution in DESs and influencing factors, and the assistance of computational approaches in understanding the interactions between DESs and lignin. DESs have manifested promising performances in lignin fractionation and valorization. The employment of DESs will be a significant approach to reduce the dependency on non-renewable resources and move towards sustainable biorefineries. Despite significant progress that has been made, additional theoretical and engineering efforts are 21 M. Zhou et al. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 156 (2022) 111986 required to understand the interactions between DESs and lignin at a molecular level, establish effective DESs recycling technologies, and developing more economically feasible lignin biorefinery strategies. With further research efforts, tunable DES systems for tailor-made lignin properties for cost-effective valorization will be expected in the near future.
